sentences.text: Six kilometres under the sea, the water will squeeze this titanium ball — with almost one lakh tonnes.
Imagine you're inside it, with two other Indians.
This ball is the heart of India's first deep-sea sub for people.
Its name is Matsya.
Your whole world is five pieces of titanium, joined by seven welds.
Now here's the strange part.
Isro is known for rockets.
But Isro's hardest weld wasn't for a rocket.
It was for this ball.
That weld was four times thicker than their welding machine could handle before.
It took about seven hundred tries.
So why was it so hard?
And after Titan, how will they know it holds?
By the end, you'll know both.

sentences.text: First, I want you to feel what six kilometres of sea actually does.

sentences.chapter: How strong is the pressure 6 km deep
sentences.text: Every ten metres you go down, the sea presses on you as hard as all the air above you.

sentences.chapter: How strong is the pressure 6 km deep

sentences.text: And again.

sentences.text: And again.

sentences.chapter: How strong is the pressure 6 km deep
sentences.text: At six thousand metres, hold out your finger.

sentences.chapter: How strong is the pressure 6 km deep
sentences.text: The water would press on your fingernail with about six hundred kilos.

sentences.chapter: How strong is the pressure 6 km deep
sentences.text: That's a full-grown buffalo, standing on one fingernail.

sentences.chapter: How strong is the pressure 6 km deep
sentences.text: Now cover the whole ball with fingernails.

sentences.chapter: How strong is the pressure 6 km deep
sentences.text: Every one of them carries a buffalo.

sentences.chapter: How strong is the pressure 6 km deep
sentences.text: Add it all up, and the sea squeezes this ball with almost one lakh tonnes, from every side at once.
So you're probably asking the same question I asked.
Could this end like Titan?
You may remember it.
In June twenty twenty-three, Titan broke apart on its way down to the Titanic.
Five people died.
Its hull, as you may know, was carbon fibre.
After earlier dives, its layers had started to come apart, and it kept diving anyway.
The U-S Coast Guard said the company's own failures caused it.
So what's different here?
Three things.
The material is titanium, the metal deep-sea subs have trusted for more than fifty years.
The shape is a ball.
And an outside inspection company checks and approves the work.
For Matsya, that company is from Norway.
And if something goes wrong down there?
The crew can drop heavy weights, and the sub rises back up.
And they carry enough air for ninety-six hours.

sentences.chapter: Why deep-sea subs use a ball
sentences.text: But why a ball?

sentences.chapter: Why deep-sea subs use a ball
sentences.text: Why not a long tube, like a normal submarine?

sentences.chapter: Why deep-sea subs use a ball
sentences.text: Squeeze a ball in your hand.

sentences.chapter: Why deep-sea subs use a ball
sentences.text: You can feel the push spread all the way round.

sentences.chapter: Why deep-sea subs use a ball
sentences.text: There's no corner and no flat side where the pressure can win.

sentences.chapter: Why deep-sea subs use a ball
sentences.text: Even America's famous deep-sea sub, Alvin, uses a ball.

sentences.chapter: Why deep-sea subs use a ball
sentences.text: Its first one, in nineteen sixty-four, was steel.

sentences.chapter: Why deep-sea subs use a ball
sentences.text: In nineteen seventy-three, they changed it to titanium, and Alvin could go almost twice as deep.

sentences.chapter: Why deep-sea subs use a ball
sentences.text: India walked the same road.

sentences.chapter: Why deep-sea subs use a ball
sentences.text: In twenty twenty-one, it lowered a test ball of plain steel six hundred metres into the Bay of Bengal.

sentences.chapter: Why deep-sea subs use a ball
sentences.text: Then came titanium.
And this, you see, is where Isro comes in.
Remember that weld I told you about?
You can't make a ball this big in one piece.
So how do you make it?
Isro's drawing shows five pieces.
A top hatch.
Three rings.
A bottom dome.
Together, they weigh about five and a half tonnes.
Seven welds join them.
Four go right round the ball, like belts.
Three go round its windows.
Here's the problem you'd face.
Titanium is fussy.
Heat it in normal air, and it grabs oxygen and nitrogen.
The weld fills with tiny holes, and it becomes weak and easy to crack.
So you can't weld it with a normal flame.
What do you do?
Isro used a beam of electrons, fired inside a vacuum.
No air, so nothing can get in.
But there was a catch.
Isro's welding centre in Bengaluru could weld up to two centimetres thick.
This wall is eight.
So they made their machine much more powerful.
Then they practised.
About seven hundred trial welds, to get the settings exactly right.
Then came the real thing.
One of the big welds that go right round the ball.
Eight centimetres deep, and about seven metres long.
It took thirty-two minutes, in one go.
Isro says it was the first time anyone in India had made a weld like this.
But then, how do you know it's good inside?
You can't cut it open, can you?
So they built X-ray machines strong enough to see through eight centimetres of titanium.
They used sound waves too, listening for hidden cracks.
And an outside agency has to certify it.

sentences.text: Now step inside with me.

sentences.chapter: Inside Matsya, and India's first aquanauts
sentences.text: The wall is eight centimetres thick, so inside, you get just over two metres.

sentences.text: Lie down in there, and your head and your feet would almost touch the walls.

sentences.text: And who will sit where you're sitting?

sentences.text: In August twenty twenty-five, India sent its first two trained people down in a French sub called Noh-teel.

sentences.chapter: Inside Matsya, and India's first aquanauts
sentences.text: Raju Ramesh, a scientist, reached about four thousand metres.

sentences.chapter: Inside Matsya, and India's first aquanauts
sentences.text: The next day, Commander Jatinder Pal Singh, a retired Navy officer, reached about five thousand.
So is Matsya ready, do you think?
Not quite.
There's one more problem.
This ball is only part of the sub.
Around it go batteries, lights, motors and arms.
Put it all together, and the whole thing sinks like a stone.
So it's wrapped in a special foam.
The foam is full of tiny hollow glass bubbles, set in hard plastic.
The titanium takes the squeeze.
The foam brings everyone home.
That foam had to come from France, and it arrived late.
Then, early this year, officials said a small crack was found in its cover.
That held up the first test dive, to five hundred metres.
On the sixth of November, Matsya finished another round of trials near Chennai, without people inside.
Officials have said the full six kilometre dive could come in twenty twenty-seven.
So why do all this, you ask?
What's down there that's worth it?
Six thousand metres down, you'd see no sunlight at all.
Your lights are the only lights for six kilometres.
Outside your window, the water is close to freezing.
And the seafloor is covered with black lumps of metal, like stones.
India has the right to explore a big patch of that seabed, in the middle of the Indian Ocean.
It has held that right since two thousand and two.
In twenty twenty-two, an Indian robot sub surveyed it, more than five kilometres down.
Those lumps hold nickel, copper and cobalt.
Metals that go into batteries, like the one in your phone.
But let me be honest with you.
Nobody is allowed to mine there yet.
The world is still writing the rules.
Matsya is not a mining machine.
It's a pair of eyes.
And you might ask, what about China?
Its sub has already taken people to the deepest point on Earth, almost eleven thousand metres.
India's first goal is six thousand, deep enough for the seabed it wants to explore.
Now, one last time, come back inside the ball with me.
I'll be straight with you.
Matsya has not been to sea with people in it yet.
And no public report says this titanium ball has been tested at full pressure yet.
So the last test will be the sea itself.
One dive.
Six kilometres.
Every number in this film, checked at once.
This story isn't over.
When Matsya makes its first deep dive, we'll be there.
